358.title: Tetzaveh: beaten olives (Exodus 27:20)
358.hook: the eternal lamp burns pure oil from crushed olives
358.howItsDone: Synagogues keep a ner tamid, an eternal light, burning above or before the ark that holds the Torah scrolls, recalling the lamp of the wilderness sanctuary; today it is often electric.

segments.voice: Yesterday Terumah ended with the ark's poles, never taken out. Your line was ready to travel. Today, a new portion, and a lamp that never goes out.

Above the ark in a synagogue, where the Torah scrolls are kept, a small light burns. Sometimes it's an old brass lamp, sometimes a modern fixture or a simple electric bulb. It's on when the room is full and when it's empty. It's on at three in the morning. It's called the ner tamid, and its story starts in this week's portion, with an instruction about olives, and about how they had to be treated to give the purest light.
screen: `A LIGHT ABOVE THE ARK.` → `ON AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `IT STARTS WITH OLIVES.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Tetzaveh, you shall command, from its first verse. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring unto thee pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually." A lamp continually: in Hebrew, ner tamid. In the wilderness sanctuary it meant the menorah, lit from evening to morning, every night, without a gap. Synagogues today keep a ner tamid of their own as a reminder. Now the oil: pure, beaten. Rashi explains that the olives were crushed in a mortar, not ground in a mill, and only the first drops were used for the light. That first oil is the clearest, with the least sediment, so it burns bright and clean; the rest could go to other uses. A midrash sees a picture in this. The prophet Jeremiah once called Israel a leafy olive tree. And the midrash says: just as an olive gives its oil only after it's beaten and crushed, so Israel, through hard times, has given light. That's a strong image, and it should be handled carefully. This midrash doesn't say suffering is good, or that pain is something to wish for. It says something more modest and more hopeful. Sometimes, after being crushed, a person or a people gives off a light they didn't know they had. A widow who starts a support group. A survivor who becomes a teacher. The pain wasn't the point. The light was what they made of it.

segments.voice: Think of someone who went through something crushing and came out giving light to others: a friend who now helps people through the same thing, a grandparent whose hard life made them gentle, maybe you. Don't make the pain smaller than it was; just notice the light and honor it. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person.
Ner tamid. The lamp that burns continually: once in the sanctuary, fed with oil from crushed olives, and now above the ark in the synagogue.
Your line: crushed olives give light. The lamp stays on, even at three in the morning. That's day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Tetzaveh: Moses' name is missing
359.hook: Moses isn't named in this portion; some link it to his offer to be blotted out for his people (Exodus 32:32)
359.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point out Moses' missing name when Tetzaveh is read; tradition also places Moses' death on the seventh of Adar, which often falls near this portion. Jewish law ranks giving anonymously among the highest forms of tzedakah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ner tamid, the lamp that burns continually, fed with oil from crushed olives. Your line was crushed olives give light. Today, still in Tetzaveh, something that isn't there.

Look closely at the credits of a big movie and you'll find hundreds of names. But the person who stayed up all night fixing the sound in one scene might not be there. The neighbor who watched the director's kids for a year definitely isn't. Since the night he was born in Egypt, Moses has been in almost every scene of the Torah: Pharaoh, the bush, the plagues, the sea, Sinai. Then comes this portion, Tetzaveh. Read it start to finish, and his name isn't in it once.
screen: `THE NAMES IN THE CREDITS.` → `THE ONES WHO AREN'T THERE.` → `TETZAVEH: NO MOSES.`

segments.voice: People who read the Torah closely have long pointed this out. From his birth in Exodus to the end of Numbers, Tetzaveh is said to be the one weekly portion where the name Moses never appears. He isn't absent, though. The portion opens, in Hebrew, v'atah tetzaveh: and you, you shall command. God is speaking to Moses the whole time. Make the oil. Dress Aaron. Ordain the priests. Moses is the you on every line, everywhere and unnamed. Why? The Torah doesn't say. A medieval commentator, the Baal HaTurim, looks ahead a few chapters, to the golden calf. After the people sin, Moses pleads for them, and says to God, in the old Jewish translation: "blot me, I pray Thee, out of Thy book which Thou hast written." Forgive them, or take my name out. The Baal HaTurim says the words of a righteous person carry weight even when said conditionally, and so his name was left out of one portion. Others notice that this portion is all about Aaron, his brother: Aaron's clothes, Aaron's sons, Aaron's role. Perhaps Moses steps back so his brother can stand in the light. Neither answer is in the text itself, but both point the same way. The greatest prophet in the Torah spends a whole portion as the unnamed you, doing the work, giving instructions that make someone else shine.

segments.voice: Think of something kind you could do where no one would know it was you: paying for someone's coffee, praising a colleague to their boss out of their hearing, giving anonymously. Picture doing it and walking away without a word. If part of you wants credit, that's normal; let it be there, and stay with the picture anyway.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. The portion where Moses is the you on every line, and his name never appears.
Your line: step out of the frame. His name can wait, and the work goes on. See you tomorrow.

360.title: Tetzaveh: clothes for splendor (Exodus 28:2)
360.hook: the priest's garments are made for splendor and for beauty, each with meaning
360.howItsDone: In synagogues that keep the custom, kohanim, men of priestly descent, still bless the congregation with the priestly blessing from Numbers 6, and a kohen is traditionally called first to the Torah reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tetzaveh, where Moses is the unnamed you on every line. Your line was step out of the frame. Today, his brother Aaron gets dressed.

A judge puts on a black robe. A surgeon scrubs and gowns. A bride spends months choosing a dress. A kid insists on wearing a superhero cape to the grocery store. Clothes don't change who we are, exactly, but they change how we stand, what others expect of us, and sometimes what we expect of ourselves. A large part of this week's portion is about clothes: what the priests of Israel wear in the sanctuary. And it starts by saying what the clothes are for.
screen: `A ROBE, A GOWN, A CAPE.` → `CLOTHES CHANGE HOW WE STAND.` → `WHAT THE CLOTHES ARE FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, for splendour and for beauty." Aaron is the kohen, the priest. A kohen served in the sanctuary, offered the sacrifices and blessed the people, and the role passed from father to son. Some Jewish families, often with names like Cohen or Kahn, keep a tradition of descent from Aaron, and in synagogues that keep the custom, kohanim still rise to give the priestly blessing. Tradition counts eight garments for the high priest: a linen tunic, linen breeches, a sash and a turban, which ordinary priests also wore in simpler form; and four of his own: a blue robe, an apron-like ephod, a breastplate set with stones, and a gold plate on the forehead. The Torah isn't shy about beauty here. It wants the clothes magnificent. But the Talmud adds a second layer: each garment atoned for a particular wrong. The tunic for bloodshed. The breeches for sexual wrongdoing. The turban for arrogance, since it sits on top. The sash, wrapped around the middle, for the thoughts of the heart. The robe, with its bells, for evil speech, a sound for a sound. The list goes on. You don't have to take it literally to see the idea: every piece of clothing can carry a meaning, a reminder of who you're trying to be.

segments.voice: Without moving much, notice what you're wearing: the fabric at your shoulders, whatever is on your feet. Pick one piece and give it a meaning, the way the Talmud gave the sash the thoughts of the heart: a collar for honest speech, shoes for walking somewhere kind.

361.title: Tetzaveh: names over the heart (Exodus 28:12, 29)
361.hook: the high priest carries the tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart
361.howItsDone: Jews pray for the sick by name, often in the Mi Sheberakh prayer said during the Torah reading, where people call out the names of those who need healing, and in the Amidah's blessing for healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kohen, the priest, dressed for splendor and for beauty. Your line was clothes carry meaning. Today, what's written on those clothes.

Some people keep a list of names. A grandmother who prays every night through her grandchildren, one by one, oldest to youngest. A nurse who keeps the first names of patients she's lost on a folded card in her wallet. A soldier with a buddy's name on a bracelet. The high priest of Israel was asked to carry an entire people this way, on his clothes, every time he went into the sanctuary. Twice over, in two different places on his body.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES.` → `ON PAPER, ON METAL.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE, ON HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: First, the shoulders. On the ephod, the high priest's apron, there are two shoulder straps, and on each sits an onyx stone. Engraved on the two stones, six and six, are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, in the order they were born. The verse says Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial. Then, the heart. Hanging in front of his chest is the breastplate, the choshen: a square of woven cloth set with twelve precious stones in four rows of three, each engraved with one tribe's name. In the old Jewish translation: "And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart." The same twelve names, carried in two places. Some readers have dwelt on the difference. The shoulders are where you carry weight: a burden, a responsibility. The heart is where you carry love: the people as people you care about. A leader needs both. Only shoulders, and the people become a weight. Only heart, and nothing gets carried. And one more thing. On the shoulders, two big stones hold six names each. On the heart, every tribe gets its own stone. Nobody is grouped. Each name is held one by one, and every time Aaron went in before God, he walked in wearing them all.

segments.voice: Let a few names come to mind, people who need carrying right now: someone sick, someone grieving, someone just starting something hard. Say each name slowly, on its own, without grouping them. If you pray, hold each one before God the way Aaron carried them; if not, let each name rest, for a breath, over your heart.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. Our portion, where the high priest carries the twelve tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart.

362.title: Tetzaveh: holy on the forehead (Exodus 28:36–38)
362.hook: a gold plate on his forehead reads "HOLY TO THE LORD"
362.howItsDone: Tetzaveh is read in synagogue once a year in the cycle of weekly portions, and its description of the high priest's garments, including the gold forehead plate, is studied with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two stones on the high priest's shoulders and twelve over his heart, each carrying a tribe's name. Your line was names on the heart. Today, one more piece of his outfit.

Where do you put the thing you most need to remember? A sticky note on the bathroom mirror. A word on your phone's lock screen. People put reminders where their eyes will land. The Torah puts one where the wearer can never see it at all. In this week's portion, Tetzaveh, the high priest gets a small plate of pure gold, tied across his forehead with a blue cord. Engraved on it, just two Hebrew words. Everyone who looks at him can read it. He can't.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `A GOLD PLATE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `EVERYONE CAN READ IT BUT HIM.`

segments.voice: The plate is called the tzitz. Exodus says to engrave it like a seal, and the words on it, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, are these: "HOLY TO THE LORD." Then comes a strange line. The plate shall be on Aaron's forehead, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, the gifts the people bring, so that they may be accepted. It shall be always upon his forehead. So the plate does work. It carries the mistakes people make even in their offerings, and it has to stay put. Why the forehead? Two days ago we heard the Talmud's list pairing each priestly garment with a wrong it helps atone for. The forehead plate, it says, is for brazenness, and it ties this to a verse in Jeremiah about a brazen forehead, the way English says someone has a nerve. The plate sits right where nerve shows, and covers it with holiness. And there's the detail from the hook: the priest can't read his own forehead. The words face out. Perhaps holiness worn on the face is mostly for the people you meet. They read it in how you look at them, long before you notice it yourself.
screen: `THE TZITZ: A PLATE OF PURE GOLD.` · `HOLY TO THE LORD.` · `THE FOREHEAD: BRAZENNESS.` · `THE WORDS FACE OUT.`

Your line: holy on the forehead. The words face out, toward everyone else. See you tomorrow.

363.title: Ki Tisa: the half shekel (Exodus 30:11–16)
363.hook: rich and poor give the same half coin; no one counts as whole alone
363.howItsDone: The half-shekel passage is read as Parashat Shekalim on the Shabbat before Adar, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of their local currency to charity in its memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gold plate engraved holy to the Lord, worn where the priest himself could never read it. Your line was holy on the forehead. Today, a new portion.

A census sounds like the dullest thing in the world. But in the Torah, a head count carries a danger: the text warns of a plague coming with the counting. So when Moses is told to count the Israelites, he's told not to count heads at all. Each one counted, from twenty years old and up, brings a coin, and the coins are counted instead. Here's the twist. The coin isn't a whole one. It's half. And the richest family in the camp and the poorest hand over exactly the same thing.
screen: `COUNT COINS, NOT HEADS.` → `EVERYONE BRINGS HALF.` → `RICH AND POOR, THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The portion is Ki Tisa, when you lift up, and the full phrase is when you lift up the head of the children of Israel: an old way of saying, when you take a count. To count someone is to lift their head. Each one gives half a shekel, an offering to the Lord, and the text adds a line worth hearing slowly. In the JPS 1917 translation: "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel." Plenty of gifts are measured by what you can afford. This one isn't. Nobody can buy a bigger share of the count, and nobody is left out for lack of money. The silver went to the service of the tent of meeting, and the text calls it a ransom for the soul, a covering, so that no plague would come with the counting. Rashi passes on a midrash: Moses couldn't picture the coin, so God showed him a coin made of fire and said, like this. And why half? The Torah doesn't say. One answer commentators give is simple: no one is complete alone. You bring your half, someone else brings theirs, and only together does anything add up. Jews still remember the half shekel. On a Shabbat just before the month of Adar, the passage is read aloud, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of the local money to charity.

segments.voice: Think of something you're part of, a family, a team, a street, a congregation, and where it's waiting on your half: a dish washed, a message answered, ten minutes of help. Don't measure it against what anyone else gives. Just picture everyone's halves adding up.
Ki Tisa. When you lift up: the portion that opens with a census counted in half coins, the same from rich and poor.
Your line: half makes a whole. Nobody gives more, nobody gives less. Day three hundred sixty-three.

364.title: Ki Tisa: Bezalel (Exodus 31:1–6)
364.hook: an artist filled "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding"
364.tomorrow: Ki Tisa: even the sanctuary rests
364.howItsDone: Bezalel's name is often invoked in Jewish life for art made in the service of holiness; the Bezalel school of art in Jerusalem, founded in 1906, is named after him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ki Tisa opened with a census counted in half coins, the same from rich and poor. Your line was half makes a whole. Today, the man who'll build it all.

Who is the first person in the Torah that God says He has filled with the spirit of God? A prophet, maybe, or a king, or Moses himself. It's none of them. Pharaoh once said the spirit of God was in Joseph, but these are God's own words, and they're about a craftsman: a man who works gold, silver and bronze, who cuts stones and carves wood. For chapters, God has described the sanctuary: the ark, the lampstand, the curtains, the priest's clothes. Somebody has to actually make it. His name is Bezalel.
screen: `FIRST FILLED WITH GOD'S SPIRIT?` → `NOT A PROPHET. A CRAFTSMAN.` → `HIS NAME IS BEZALEL.`

segments.voice: God says to Moses, see, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And in the JPS 1917 translation: "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." The Torah puts skilled hands on the same list as the spirit of God. His name helps. Bezalel can be read as in the shadow of God, and the Talmud, in Berakhot, tells a story built on it. Moses gives Bezalel the instructions starting with the ark and the furniture, and only then the tent. Bezalel answers: usually a person builds the house first and then brings the furniture in. Moses says: you must have been standing in the shadow of God, because that's exactly the order God told me. The same page says Bezalel knew how to join the letters by which heaven and earth were made: a craftsman with the knowledge of creation in his fingers. And he isn't alone. God gives him a partner, Oholiab, from the tribe of Dan. Rashi notes that Dan was among the humblest tribes, and Judah among the greatest: the sanctuary was made by both together. So a week of the sanctuary and its people ends: crushed olives for light, Moses stepping out of the frame, clothes that carry meaning, names on the heart, holy on the forehead, half a coin each, and now the artist with his hands full of spirit.
screen: `FILLED WITH THE SPIRIT OF GOD.` · `IN THE SHADOW OF GOD.` · `THE LETTERS OF CREATION.` · `JUDAH AND DAN, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `CRAFT IS SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Make something small with your hands: fold a piece of paper into a shape, sketch the cup in front of you, tie a careful knot. Do it slowly and watch your fingers work, the small choices, the moment it comes out right. If you pray, offer the work as it is; if not, just let your hands be fully here.
Ki Tisa. The portion where God names Bezalel, the craftsman filled with the spirit of God and the skill of his hands.
Your line: craft is spirit. Skilled hands sit on the same list as wisdom. That's day three hundred sixty-four.

chat.says: Was Bezalel a prophet? Why does God say he's filled with the spirit of God?
options: He was a craftsman; the Torah puts skilled workmanship on the same list as God's spirit.
He was a priest, and the spirit came on him only once he put on Aaron's garments.
He was Moses' scribe, filled with spirit so he could copy the tablets exactly.
